notes: Mass-bred stock has widespread defects; "neon tetra disease" is untreatable at an advanced stage. Prefers dim light with plants and floaters.
"Very peaceful indeed". An unreserved newcomer recommendation with "no special demands" on water chemistry.
Kept permanently warm, its lifespan shortens.
SF: "generally very peaceful". ACO: barbs as a group can be semi-aggressive; buy 6+ and keep away from long-finned fish. pH range is for farmed fish.
"One of the hardiest small cyprinids". Some forms reach 3.5–3.9 in.
Mid-to-upper levels; does not normally hunt fry. A shrimp-safe nano fish.
SF sizes a group for a 20 gal long (30 × 12 in). Dyed specimens are sold. Group size and fin-nipping verdict not found in source.
Shy; males spar but not toward tankmates; rarely rises to the surface. SF: group "ideally 20 or more". Avoid tannins. New imports are often in poor condition.
Dyed and short-body mutants are sold. Needs sinking food. ACO gives a group of 3–6.
Temperature range is for tank-bred fish. Kept above 77°F long-term, "lifespan will be reduced considerably". Usually smaller than 2 in.
Very peaceful; preferably 10+. Angelfish, gouramis and larger catfish eat it, so it is not for a general community.
Sold as P. kuhlii. Nocturnal; may eat eggs or fry. Buries itself and jumps. ACO calls it beginner-friendly and gives a group of 3–6.
Keep one, or a pair; territorial with its own kind. Often misidentified. The small-tank alternative to the common pleco.
Slow and easily intimidated; groups form a hierarchy. SF (pygmy cory page) lists gouramis among fish that eat pygmy corys.
One male. SF: "Not recommended for the standard community aquarium". ACO: 5 gal alone, OK with tetras or corys in 10+ gal. pH range is for ornamental strains.
Avoid fin-nipping tankmates. Commercial stock is inbred. Group size not found.
Best for beginners "as long as the ph remains above neutral". Keep more females than males.
Males about 1 in, females 1.8 in. Too small for a general community; crossbreeds with guppies. Keep several females.
Shy and territorial; a male and female pair, never two males. SF gives only a "reserved recommendation" because of health issues. pH range is for tank-bred fish.

Prey for any fish that fits it in its mouth. Low GH causes failed molts. Copper is "lethal to all invertebrates". Overfeeding is "the #1 cause" of deaths. Belongs in "a mature tank that has been running for many months". ShrimpKeepers: active soil "can lower pH too much".
"Super hardy" algae eater; wants "moderate to hard GH". Outcompetes cherry shrimp for food, escapes (needs a lid) and cannot breed in freshwater. Fits "most nano tanks".
Needs "lots of minerals"; shells crack in soft water. Plant-safe and won't overpopulate, but starves when algae runs out. ACO: 2–3 gal.
Eats duckweed and other floaters; may uproot plants in loose substrate. Shell pitting in soft water. 5 gal for 1–2 snails.

Keep as a pair; male 3 in, female 2 in. Bred fish are "relatively unfussy" on pH; wild fish may need pH 5.0–6.0 to breed. Females "hyper-aggressive" after spawning in small tanks. Small weekly water changes, gentle flow. Dwarf pencilfish make good dither fish.
Needs "pristine water quality"; HLLE-like erosion in poor water. Avoid most other cichlids.
Single or pair in a 90 × 45 cm base; a group of 6–8 needs 120 cm+. Gravel "can inhibit feeding".

ACO: "Most are pretty aggressive and territorial"; 5 gal plus 3 per extra puffer ("six to seven… in a 20-gallon"); 1 male to 2–3 females. SF: 2–3 gal each. Rejects dried food; very sensitive to water quality. Best in a species-only tank; results with shrimp are mixed. Sources disagree on whether snails are needed to wear down its teeth.

Micropredator: small live or frozen food, no bloodworm. Rival males are "very aggressive"; keep one male, a pair, or a male with several females. Easily outcompeted, so only small, calm mid-water tankmates.
Shrimp-compatible. Should not be fed dried food only.
A pair or small group. Some keepers report it "preys on small freshwater shrimp". Jumps; needs a lid and a humid air layer. Gentle flow.
Colour fades in poor or alkaline water; weekly water changes "are a must".
Ideally 10+. Males' long fins get nipped. Tiny mouth; mostly live food. Good with pygmy corys, otos, Pseudomugil and shrimp.
Robust but "not suitable for the general community"; a "prodigious jumper", so a tight lid. 2–3 females per male. A good first killifish. Tank size not recorded by the source.
Hardness range is for the ornamental strain. Mostly live food. Shrimp-compatible.
Middle to upper levels; "does not actively predate fry". An ideal dither fish for Apistogramma.
Needs 15–20× turnover, high oxygen and algae-covered rock in a mature tank. Climbs glass. Often sold emaciated.

Covers O. vittatus, O. macrospilus and O. cocama; the tank size is from SF's zebra oto (O. cocama) page. Mostly wild-caught and arrives starved; "a couple of plump and healthy otos" beats a starving school. SF: "should never be added to an immature aquarium".

Needs RO water remineralized with GH-only salts and an active buffering substrate; ADA-type soils buffer pH to about 6.6–6.8 for 12–18 months. Above 78°F brings "stress, reduced breeding, shortened lifespan". New active soil leaches ammonia; allow 4–6 weeks of cycling. "If you set up a tank for Neocaridina and add Caridina, the Caridina will die." TDS 100–150 ppm. Fast Aquatics recommends no fish for breeding colonies.
